text: A fix nobody wrote down is a fix nobody can learn from — including future-you, staring at this index in six months wondering why it exists. This lesson applies real documentation habits to a real write-up.

Five short sections serve a manager and the next DBA at once: summary, symptom, root cause, change made, and result. The change-made section carries the exact CREATE INDEX and DROP INDEX statements verbatim — not paraphrased — because anyone auditing this later needs the real T-SQL.

The result section carries the verified numbers directly: duration twenty-eight thousand milliseconds down to eighty-five, logical reads a hundred eighteen thousand down to three hundred fifty, PAGEIOLATCH_SH waits for this query effectively eliminated, no write-side regression.

A manager leans on the summary and result — plain language, one number, one date. A DBA leans on root cause and the actual change — the plan detail, the real DDL, and a caveat about what this fix does and doesn't cover. Same facts, two depths, never two different stories.
"We added an index" expires the moment someone forgets why. "Key Lookups scale with account size — check for this pattern elsewhere" keeps paying off. Next up: wrapping up the whole capstone.
